1212.title: Faith in mind
1212.hook: a Chan poem attributed to the third patriarch Sengcan: the great way is not hard for those without picking and choosing
1212.howItsDone: In some Zen and Chan communities the Xinxin Ming is chanted or recited in services and studied in talks, and students often learn its opening lines by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shikantaza: just sitting, with no object at all, the way Dogen taught it. Your line: just this.

The great way is not difficult. That's how the poem opens, and for half a line it sounds like very good news. Then comes the condition: it is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose. Which can describe a whole morning. Coffee or tea. Skip this song. That email can wait, this one can't. The poem is short and plain, built from paired lines that sound almost like proverbs, and some Chan and Zen students chant it and carry it. Tradition credits it to Sengcan, remembered in the Chan lineage as the third ancestor, counting Bodhidharma as the first.
screen: `THE GREAT WAY IS NOT DIFFICULT.` → `EXCEPT FOR ONE THING.` → `A POEM CARRIED BY CHAN.`

segments.voice: In Chinese the title is Xinxin Ming, often given in English as Faith in Mind, or Trust in Mind. The two words read xin are different. The first means trust or faith. The second means heart-mind, the whole of what thinks and feels. So this faith isn't faith in a creed. Some readers hear it as trust that the mind, as it is, is already enough to meet the way. In paraphrase, the poem goes on: when love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and open. The way isn't hidden. Something stands in front of it, and the poem names it: the habit of grabbing at one side and pushing away the other. That doesn't mean stop having taste. You can still notice that the tea is too strong. What the poem calls the sickness of the mind is setting what you like against what you dislike, turning every small preference into a quiet war. Rain on the day of a picnic is rain. The poem's interest is in everything piled on top of the rain. And why faith? The poem describes the way as round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking and nothing extra. Only taking and rejecting, it says, keeps it from being seen so. Yesterday's just sitting is this same trust done with the body: no target, no improvement project. The poem puts that trust into words.
screen: `THE TITLE: FAITH IN MIND.` · `NOT HIDDEN, JUST BLOCKED.` · `TASTE IS FINE; THE WAR IS NOT.` · `ROUND AND COMPLETE, LIKE SPACE.` · then, large: `NO PICKING AND CHOOSING.`

segments.voice: For this sit, take what the body brings, an itch on the cheek, a stiff knee, cool air on the hands, each with an urge attached to scratch, shift or fix it. You don't need to obey the urge or fight it; see it as a preference, and let the sensation be a sensation for a few breaths. If you do need to move, move slowly, knowing you chose.
Xinxin Ming. The Chan poem whose title is often rendered Faith in Mind, and which opens: the great way is not difficult for those who don't pick and choose. Today's word.
Your line: no picking and choosing. Taste can stay; the war can go. Until next time.

1213.title: Hair's breadth
1213.hook: the poem: a hair's breadth of difference and heaven and earth are set apart
1213.howItsDone: Zen and Chan teachers often quote this line of the Xinxin Ming in talks to point at how quickly a small preference becomes a large separation, and students use it as a reminder during sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Xinxin Ming, faith in mind: the great way is not difficult, for those who don't pick and choose. Your line: no picking and choosing.

A ship leaves harbor with its wheel turned the smallest bit off true. From the dock, nobody could see it. A day out, the coast still looks right. But keep sailing, across a whole ocean, and that ship comes ashore on a different coast from the one it meant to reach. The turn was tiny. The distance it opens is not. Yesterday's poem has a line built on exactly this shape: the smallest gap, the largest distance.
screen: `A SHIP LEAVES HARBOR.` → `THE WHEEL, A HAIR OFF TRUE.` → `A DIFFERENT COAST.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the Xinxin Ming says: if there is the slightest difference, a hair's breadth, then heaven and earth are set apart. It comes a few lines after the opening, so it isn't a new subject. It's the same warning about picking and choosing, now with a picture of how big the cost can grow. It can sound like a call to be exacting: a hair's breadth off and you've failed. But that reading turns the line into one more round of picking and choosing, right against wrong, perfect against flawed. The difference the poem means is the split the mind makes between what is here and what it wants instead. That split usually opens very small. A name lights up on your phone and, before you read a word, there's a flicker. Ugh. Or a flicker of yes, this one I like. No story yet, no argument, just a lean. That lean is the hair's breadth. Why heaven and earth? The poem pairs the smallest thing it can name with the largest. It isn't threatening anyone. It's describing distance. A tiny lean, held and fed, tilts the whole conversation, then the whole relationship, the way a hair off on the wheel puts a ship on another coast. And the line has a gentler side. If the gap begins as a hair, it can also be noticed while it is still only a hair wide.

1214.title: Don't seek the true
1214.hook: the poem: don't seek the true, just stop holding opinions
1214.howItsDone: In Zen and Chan practice this line is sometimes quoted in talks and used during sitting as a reminder to let commentary about the sitting, and about everything else, go by without holding on to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hair's breadth: the smallest lean of liking and disliking, and heaven and earth set apart. Your line: a hair's breadth.

How many opinions have you held since you woke up? About the weather. The traffic. Someone's haircut, a headline, the way the coffee came out. Nobody asked for most of them, and plenty are gone by lunch. They arrive on their own, like notifications. Now here is a religious poem, chanted in some Chan and Zen halls, and in the middle of it comes a line that sounds almost backwards. You might expect it to say: seek the truth with all your heart. It says the opposite.
screen: `OPINIONS SINCE BREAKFAST.` → `A RELIGIOUS POEM.` → `A LINE THAT SOUNDS BACKWARDS.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the Xinxin Ming says: do not seek the true; just stop holding opinions. A startling thing to put in a poem about the way. Isn't truth the point? Look at the word just. The poem isn't saying truth doesn't matter. It's saying that hunting for it, as if it were a prize somewhere else, is one more kind of grabbing, one more round of picking and choosing. The poem has already called the way round and complete, like vast space, with nothing lacking. So the instruction isn't go and find it. It's stop doing the thing that covers it. Then, holding versus having. Opinions will keep arriving; the line doesn't ask you to stop thinking. It asks you to stop clutching. An opinion you can set down is a thought. One you can't set down has become a wall, and you end up seeing the wall instead of the person, the movie, the rainy afternoon. Yesterday's hair's breadth was the first lean. An opinion is that lean after it has set hard. And what's left when you put one down? Not emptiness. The thing itself, unedited. The coworker, before your verdict on her. The song, before you decided it was overplayed. The poem's wager is that this plain thing, without commentary, is closer to what you were seeking in the first place.
screen: `THE LINE: DON'T SEEK THE TRUE.` · `THE KEY WORD IS 'JUST'.` · `HOLDING, NOT HAVING.` · `THE THING ITSELF, UNEDITED.` · then, large: `JUST STOP HOLDING OPINIONS.`

segments.voice: Within a few breaths, a comment will show up about the sitting itself: this is going well, I'm bad at this, my knee. Those are opinions too, so each time one comes, see it and set it down, the way you'd set a cup on a table. You don't have to argue with it.
Don't seek the true. The Xinxin Ming's line that turns the search around: don't hunt for truth somewhere else, just stop holding opinions. Today's word.
Your line: just stop holding opinions. Thoughts still come; they just don't have to be clutched. More of the poem tomorrow.

1215.title: Faith and mind, not two
1215.hook: the poem ends: faith and mind are not two
1215.carry: not two, and not clinging to one
1215.howItsDone: Zen and Chan students who chant the Xinxin Ming end on these lines, and some teachers offer 'not two' as a phrase to return to in sitting when the mind starts to divide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that turns the search around: don't seek the true. Your line: just stop holding opinions.

Some poems save their biggest image for the last line: a sunset, a storm, a door closing. The Xinxin Ming does something stranger. It ends by taking its own title, faith and mind, and folding the two words together until there is no gap between them. After all the warnings, about picking and choosing, the hair's breadth, the opinions, the last word it leaves is a pair of plain words. Not two.
screen: `SOME POEMS END ON AN IMAGE.` → `THIS ONE FOLDS ITS TITLE.` → `TWO PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the poem closes: faith and mind are not two; not two is faith in mind. Then it says the way is beyond words, not a matter of past, future or present. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say faith and mind are one. Why not? Because one is just another thing to hold. Earlier the poem has a line for exactly this: two exists because of one, so don't cling even to the one. Chinese Buddhist texts use this word, not two, for what English often calls nonduality, and its whole job is to stop the mind landing anywhere: not split into two, and not stuck on one either. It's also practical. In paraphrase, the poem advises: if you want to come into accord with the way quickly, just say: not two. Some translators add, when doubt arises. It's less a doctrine to agree with than a tool to use, right when the mind starts dividing the moment into what I want and what I don't. And the title folds shut. The poem began with picking and choosing, the mind splitting its day into liked and disliked. It ends with the trust and the mind that trusts refusing to come apart. No faith standing over here, aimed at a mind over there. In the poem's last breath, the trusting and the trusted are not two. Back where the week started: the great way is not hard.
screen: `THE LAST LINES: NOT TWO.` · `NOT TWO IS NOT 'ONE'.` · `TO ACCORD QUICKLY, SAY IT.` · `THE TITLE, FOLDED SHUT.` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

1216.title: The Platform Sutra
1216.hook: the teachings of Huineng, the sixth patriarch, as his students remembered them
1216.howItsDone: In Zen and Chan communities the Platform Sutra is studied, and the story of Huineng's arrival and the two verses on the wall is retold in talks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of the Xinxin Ming: faith and mind are not two. Your line: not two.

A young man is selling firewood in a market town in the far south of China. He's poor. The sutra says his father died when he was small, and he and his mother live on what the wood brings in. He delivers a bundle to a customer's lodging, and on his way out he hears a man inside reciting a sutra, the Diamond Sutra. He stops. Something in him opens at the words. He asks where the man learned it: a monastery to the north, where a teacher named Hongren teaches. The young man's name is Huineng.
screen: `FIREWOOD IN A SOUTHERN MARKET.` → `A SUTRA THROUGH A DOORWAY.` → `A TEACHER TO THE NORTH.`

segments.voice: The Platform Sutra presents itself as Huineng's own talks, given from a teaching seat, a raised platform, at a temple, and written down by his students. It opens with him telling his life, starting with the firewood. Huineng arrives at Hongren's monastery and asks to become a Buddha. Hongren tests him: you're from the south, a barbarian, he says, using a rough word for southern people. How could you become a Buddha? Huineng answers: people may be northern or southern, but Buddha-nature has no north or south. Hongren says nothing more for the moment and sends him to the back to split wood and pound rice. Then, two verses on a wall. Hongren asks his monks to write a verse showing what they've understood. The senior monk, Shenxiu, writes, in paraphrase: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it again and again, and let no dust settle. Huineng can't read or write, the sutra says, so he asks someone to put his verse up beside it. In one widely retold version: awakening has no tree, the mirror has no stand; from the beginning there is not one thing, so where would dust settle? Hongren calls him in secret, teaches him at night, and names him his heir, and so tradition calls Huineng the sixth patriarch. The rest of the Platform Sutra is his teaching, and the coming days are spent inside it.
screen: `TALKS FROM A TEACHING SEAT.` · `NO NORTH OR SOUTH IN BUDDHA-NATURE.` · `TWO VERSES ON A WALL.` · `HONGREN'S HEIR.` · then, large: `THE SIXTH PATRIARCH.`

segments.voice: Huineng's story begins with the plainest line he could give: a poor boy, a widowed mother, a load of firewood. Let the first plain line of your own story come up, the way you'd tell it if you weren't trying to impress anyone, and hear it once without polishing it. Then let it go, and rest in the breath, carrying no bundle at all.
The Platform Sutra. The teachings of Huineng, told from a teaching seat and remembered by his students, opening with his own story. Today's word.
Your line: the sixth patriarch. A woodcutter from the south, and a Buddha-nature with no north or south. Rest well.

1217.title: No-thought
1217.hook: Huineng: no-thought is not blankness but not being stuck to thoughts
1217.howItsDone: Zen and Chan teachers often explain Huineng's no-thought in talks on sitting, describing practice as letting thoughts arise and pass without being carried off, rather than forcing the mind blank.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Platform Sutra: a woodcutter from the south who became, as tradition calls him, the sixth patriarch. Your line: the sixth patriarch.

A big station has a departures board. Every few minutes it clicks over: a new train, a new platform, a new city. Nobody standing in the hall gets on every train. Most people glance up, read a line, and keep walking. Some trains they board. Most they let go, and the board doesn't mind either way. Now try that with a mind. Thoughts click over all day: lunch, that email, a worry about Thursday. Huineng had a word for meeting them the way a traveler meets a departures board, and it's probably not what it sounds like.
screen: `A DEPARTURES BOARD.` → `NOBODY BOARDS EVERY TRAIN.` → `THOUGHTS CLICK OVER ALL DAY.`

segments.voice: In the Platform Sutra, Huineng sets out three teachings side by side: no-thought as the doctrine, no-form as the substance, and non-abiding as the root. Today is the first, but they lean on each other. No-thought sounds like an empty head, a mind wiped blank. Huineng says plainly that this is a mistake. Trying to think of nothing at all, cutting off every thought, is in his telling its own kind of trap, a mind tied up by an idea of what meditation should be. So what is it? In paraphrase, he says no-thought means that in the midst of thoughts, you are not carried off by them. Thought follows thought, and none of them is held on to. That's the non-abiding: the mind doesn't move in and live in any one of them. When thoughts don't stick, he says, there is no bondage. So the worry about Thursday can arrive, can even be useful, and then go, the way a train leaves the board. And the senses stay open. Huineng doesn't ask anyone to close their eyes on the world. He describes the senses going out and coming back freely, seeing and hearing everything, while the mind isn't stained by what it meets. No-thought, in his hands, isn't less life. It's full life, with nothing gripping. The same thread the Xinxin Ming was pulling a few days ago, now tied to a teacher's seat: not stuck.
screen: `THREE TEACHINGS, ONE STRAND.` · `NOT A BLANK MIND.` · `THOUGHT AFTER THOUGHT, UNSTUCK.` · `THE SENSES COME AND GO FREELY.` · then, large: `NOT STUCK.`

segments.voice: Don't try to stop thinking; let thoughts come up like lines on a departures board, notice each one, there's a thought, and let it go on without you. If you find you've boarded one and are a few stops down the line in a story, that's fine. Just step off and come back to the breath.

1218.title: Sudden awakening
1218.hook: Huineng's southern school taught that awakening is sudden; the northern school stressed the gradual
1218.howItsDone: Zen and Chan schools discuss sudden and gradual awakening in talks and study, and some teachers present them as two sides of practice rather than rival paths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no-thought: thoughts come and go, and the mind isn't carried off. Your line: not stuck.

Anyone who learned to ride a bike can tell it two ways. One way: it took weeks. Scraped knees, a hand on the back of the seat, more wobbly starts than anyone counted. The other way: it happened in an instant. One afternoon the hand let go, and suddenly you were riding. Both stories are true, told from different ends. Chan Buddhism in China told its own version of this argument, about awakening, and attached it to two teachers already met at the wall with their verses.
screen: `IT TOOK WEEKS.` → `IT HAPPENED IN AN INSTANT.` → `BOTH STORIES ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: The Platform Sutra speaks of a southern teaching and a northern one: Huineng in the south, Shenxiu in the north. It links the south with sudden awakening and the north with the gradual. The verses show the two emphases. Shenxiu's said: wipe the mirror again and again, let no dust settle. That's patient, steady practice, a little cleaner each day. Huineng's answered: from the beginning there is nothing for dust to land on. That's seeing, all at once, what was already so. Then the surprise: the sutra doesn't let the argument end there. In paraphrase, Huineng says the teaching itself is neither sudden nor gradual. People are quicker or slower, and that is where the difference lies. The way is one. The pace belongs to the walker. Read like that, sudden and gradual aren't rival camps. They're the bike story told from both ends: the long wobbling, and the instant it clicks. And this week has had both in it. The Xinxin Ming: the great way is not hard, without picking and choosing. A hair's breadth, and heaven and earth apart. Don't seek the true, just stop holding opinions. Not two. A woodcutter who heard a sutra through a doorway. No-thought, not stuck. Any one of those can land in an instant. Any one of them can also take years of mornings to live.
screen: `SOUTH SUDDEN, NORTH GRADUAL.` · `TWO VERSES, TWO EMPHASES.` · `THE TEACHING HAS NO SPEEDS.` · `A WEEK OF BOTH.` · then, large: `SUDDEN AND GRADUAL.`

segments.voice: Notice that each breath arrives whole, all at once, the moment it's here, and that the sitting settles slowly, a little at a time; let both be true. Then bring to mind someone whose pace differs from yours, who goes slowly where you rush or leaps where you plod. Hold them in mind for a few breaths with some respect, as another walker on the same road.
